title: Birds & Botanicals
description: The art of scientific observation — Audubon's birds and the great botanical plates.

items.title: American Flamingo
items.cultural_context: Plate 431 of The Birds of America, the culminating plate of Audubon's double-elephant-folio masterwork, engraved and hand-colored by Robert Havell Jr. in London.
items.description_narrative: Audubon posed the flamingo with its head lowered to fit the towering flock's bill within the folio's giant page, its neck forming a graceful arc against a Florida Keys shoreline. The plate is among the most recognized images in American natural-history art.

items.title: Wild Turkey
items.cultural_context: Plate 1 of The Birds of America, chosen to open the series as a proud emblem of American wildlife; based on a bird Audubon observed in Louisiana.
items.description_narrative: A male wild turkey strides through cane and grass in full display, rendered life-size as Audubon's working method demanded. It was the first plate published and set the ambitious visual standard for the entire folio.

items.title: Snowy Heron or White Egret
items.cultural_context: Plate 242 of The Birds of America, depicting a species later devastated by the plume trade that spurred early American bird-conservation movements.
items.description_narrative: The snowy egret is shown in full breeding plumage, its delicate aigrette feathers fanned out along a marshy shoreline. Those same plumes made the species a prime target of the 19th-century feather trade Audubon's images later helped condemn.

items.title: Carolina Parakeet
items.cultural_context: Plate 26 of The Birds of America, portraying North America's only native parrot species, which was declared extinct in the early 20th century.
items.description_narrative: Seven Carolina parakeets cluster and feed on cocklebur seed heads, their green, yellow, and orange plumage rendered in vivid detail. The species vanished from the wild within decades of this plate's publication, making it a haunting record of a lost bird.

items.title: Great Blue Heron
items.cultural_context: Plate 211 of The Birds of America, one of many wading-bird studies Audubon made along the Gulf Coast and southeastern wetlands.
items.description_narrative: A great blue heron stands poised at the water's edge, its long neck coiled in the characteristic hunting posture Audubon observed firsthand in the field. The composition balances scientific precision with a painterly sense of stillness.

items.title: White-headed Eagle (Bald Eagle)
items.cultural_context: Plate 31 of The Birds of America, depicting the bird Audubon controversially described feeding on a catfish carcass rather than in noble flight.
items.description_narrative: Audubon shows a bald eagle tearing at a catfish on a riverbank, a deliberately unromantic scene that drew criticism for undermining the bird's symbolic dignity. The plate remains a landmark in his effort to depict raptors from direct observation rather than convention.

items.title: Whooping Crane
items.cultural_context: Plate 226 of The Birds of America, depicting one of North America's rarest cranes, whose population would later collapse to a few dozen birds by the mid-20th century.
items.description_narrative: Two whooping cranes forage in a wetland, their brilliant white plumage and red-capped heads set against a muted marsh background. Audubon's record predates the species' near-extinction and subsequent conservation recovery by over a century.

items.title: Rosa Centifolia (Cabbage Rose)
items.description_narrative: A cabbage rose plate from Redouté's landmark folio Les Roses, the artist celebrated as the 'Raphael of flowers' for his work at the court of Empress Joséphine. His stipple-engraving technique rendered petals with a luminous, almost photographic delicacy.
items.tags: rose, botanical, redoute, les roses, flower, engraving, french

items.title: Rosa Gallica
items.description_narrative: The French rose, Rosa gallica, as engraved for Redouté's Les Roses, the most famous botanical rose book ever produced. The plate pairs scientific precision with the refined elegance that made Redouté the favored flower painter of Napoleonic France.
items.tags: rose, botanical, redoute, les roses, gallica, engraving, french

items.title: Lilium Candidum (Madonna Lily)
items.description_narrative: The Madonna lily from Redouté's monumental Les Liliacées, an eight-volume survey of lilies and related plants produced under the patronage of Empress Joséphine. Its pure white blooms are rendered with the stipple technique that let Redouté capture subtle gradations of tone.
items.tags: lily, botanical, redoute, les liliacees, madonna lily, engraving, french

items.title: Dalmatian Iris (Iris Pallida)
items.description_narrative: Plate 366 from volume seven of Redouté's Les Liliacées depicts the Dalmatian iris, Iris pallida, engraved by De Gouy after the master's drawing. The soft lavender falls and standards showcase the delicate color modeling that defined the Redouté school.
items.tags: iris, botanical, redoute, les liliacees, flower, engraving, french

items.title: Kunstformen der Natur: Nepenthaceae (Pitcher Plants)
items.description_narrative: Plate 62 of Ernst Haeckel's Kunstformen der Natur, arranging carnivorous pitcher plants into a symmetrical, ornamental composition. Haeckel, a biologist and artist, used such plates to argue that nature's forms were the source of aesthetic order.
items.tags: nepenthes, pitcher plant, haeckel, kunstformen, botanical, lithograph, german

items.title: Kunstformen der Natur: Trochilidae (Hummingbirds)
items.description_narrative: A plate of hummingbirds from Ernst Haeckel's Kunstformen der Natur, their iridescent plumage arranged in Haeckel's signature radiating symmetry. The work fused rigorous zoological observation with the decorative sensibility that influenced Art Nouveau.
items.tags: hummingbird, trochilidae, haeckel, kunstformen, natural history, lithograph, german

items.title: Kunstformen der Natur: Discomedusae (Jellyfish)
items.description_narrative: Haeckel's celebrated jellyfish plate from Kunstformen der Natur, depicting disc-shaped medusae with trailing tentacles in flowing, symmetrical arrangement. This image is among the most iconic of the collection and directly inspired Art Nouveau designers.
items.tags: jellyfish, medusae, haeckel, kunstformen, marine, lithograph, german

items.title: Kunstformen der Natur: Chiroptera (Bats)
items.description_narrative: Plate 67 of Ernst Haeckel's Kunstformen der Natur presents a study of bats, their expressive faces and membranous wings composed into an ordered panel. Haeckel's morphological plates emphasized the underlying symmetry he saw uniting all living forms.
items.tags: bat, chiroptera, haeckel, kunstformen, natural history, lithograph, german

items.title: Kunstformen der Natur: Actiniae (Sea Anemones)
items.description_narrative: Sea anemones rendered in vivid color for Ernst Haeckel's Kunstformen der Natur, their radial bodies and tentacles arranged as a decorative tableau. The plate exemplifies Haeckel's belief that scientific illustration could reveal nature's inherent artistry.
items.tags: sea anemone, actiniae, haeckel, kunstformen, marine, lithograph, german

items.title: Pineapple with Cockroaches
items.description_narrative: A pineapple plate from Maria Sibylla Merian's Metamorphosis insectorum Surinamensium, the pioneering study she produced after a self-funded expedition to Dutch Surinam. Merian was among the first naturalists to document insects alongside their host plants and full life cycles.
items.tags: pineapple, insects, merian, surinam, metamorphosis, engraving, botanical

items.title: Magnolia Grandiflora
items.description_narrative: Georg Dionysius Ehret's magnolia, plate 33 from Plantae Selectae, produced with the botanist Christoph Jacob Trew. Ehret was the foremost botanical artist of the eighteenth century, and his large-format magnolia is among the most admired flower engravings of the era.
items.tags: magnolia, ehret, plantae selectae, botanical, flower, engraving, german

items.title: Red Poppy
items.description_narrative: A red poppy plate from Elizabeth Blackwell's A Curious Herbal, which she drew, engraved, and hand-colored herself to raise funds to free her husband from debtors' prison. The herbal documented medicinal plants of the age and made Blackwell a rare woman botanical author of her century.
items.tags: poppy, blackwell, curious herbal, medicinal, botanical, engraving, british

items.title: Superb Lyrebird
items.description_narrative: The superb lyrebird from John Gould's The Birds of Australia, the seven-volume work that introduced many Australian species to European science. The plates were lithographed largely from the field studies of Gould's wife and collaborator, Elizabeth Gould.
items.tags: lyrebird, bird, gould, birds of australia, ornithology, lithograph, british

items.title: Ivory-billed Woodpecker
items.description_narrative: The now-critically-endangered ivory-billed woodpecker, plate 16 from Mark Catesby's The Natural History of Carolina, Florida and the Bahama Islands. Catesby's folio was the first published account of the flora and fauna of British North America, and he etched most of the plates himself.
items.tags: woodpecker, bird, catesby, carolina, ornithology, engraving, american
